Umbrij command-line switches (-deepsearch / -runas-currentuser / -debugport / -domainAd / -savepdf) AIExploitation High
Hunts execution of the Umbrij tool by its distinctive command-line parameters documented in the article, including the example invocation of a renamed BDSubWiz.exe with -regex and -deepsearch. These switch names are unique to Umbrij. Rationale: Anchors on the verbatim Umbrij CLI parameters enumerated in the article's parameter table (-deepsearch, -runas-currentuser, -domainAd, -savepdf, -debugport, -browser). These switch spellings are tool-specific and not used by mainstream software, giving very high fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/
ATT&CKT1528 T1134.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A bespoke internal automation tool that happens to use a -debugport plus -browser flag combination
  • Red-team replaying Umbrij invocations during an authorized engagement
  • An unrelated CLI utility using the generic -savepdf flag (mitigated by requiring the ToddyCat-specific switch set)
  • Developer testing of a custom .NET tool with similar argument naming
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full command line and the executing binary; resolve which browser/path/port were targeted (-path, -browser, -debugport) and whether -runas-currentuser/-user indicates token impersonation. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process, and revoke/rotate the affected user's Google OAuth sessions and tokens immediately. 3) Hunt: correlate with the parent sideload host (BDS.exe/log.dll), Chromium --remote-debugging-port launches, and outbound *.googleapis.com traffic on the same host and account.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-deepsearch","-runas-currentuser","-domainAd","-savepdf")
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "-debugport" and ProcessCommandLine has "-browser")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has_any ("-deepsearch","-runas-currentuser","-domainAd","-savepdf")
   or (CommandLine has "-debugport" and CommandLine has "-browser")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

Chromium browser launched headless with --remote-debugging-port by a non-browser parent (STRD) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the core Shadow-Token-via-Remote-Debug step: Umbrij launches Chrome/Edge/Chromium with a remote debugging port (often headless) to drive the user's live Gmail session. Flags browser processes carrying --remote-debugging-port when spawned by the sideload hosts or run headless. Rationale: Built on the article's explicit description of launching a Chromium browser in headless mode and connecting via the remote debugging port; pairs the --remote-debugging-port flag with the article-specific sideload parents or the --headless evasion flag to suppress legitimate interactive debugging. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/ • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0228/
ATT&CKT1185 T1528
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers/QA running Selenium/Puppeteer/Playwright automation with --remote-debugging-port and --headless
  • CI build agents driving headless Chrome for screenshot or PDF generation
  • VS Code / IDE debugging a web app via the Chrome DevTools Protocol
  • Synthetic monitoring agents launching headless browsers
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Microsoft VS Code" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("node.exe","devenv.exe","chromedriver.exe","msedgedriver.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the parent process and folder — a CI/automation tool from a dev path is likely benign; a browser spawned by BDSubWiz/bds/GoogleDesktop or from Users\Public/Temp is malicious. Note the --remote-debugging-port value and target profile. 2) Contain: isolate host, terminate the browser and parent, and immediately revoke the user's Google sessions/refresh tokens and force re-auth. 3) Hunt: pivot to outbound *.googleapis.com / accounts.google.com connections from the same host/account and to the Umbrij CLI-switch and log.dll sideload detections.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","chromium.exe","brave.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("BDSubWiz.exe","bds.exe","VSTestVideoRecorder.exe","GoogleDesktop.exe")
     or ProcessCommandLine has "--headless"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\chrome.exe", @"\msedge.exe", @"\chromium.exe", @"\brave.exe")
| where CommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port"
| where ParentProcessName has_any (@"\BDSubWiz.exe", @"\bds.exe", @"\VSTestVideoRecorder.exe", @"\GoogleDesktop.exe")
     or CommandLine has "--headless"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

Sideload-host binary connecting to Google OAuth/Gmail API endpoints (token exchange) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the credential-access/exfil step where Umbrij (running as a renamed signed binary, not a browser) exchanges the stolen OAuth authorization code for an access token and pulls Gmail via the Google API. Flags the sideload hosts contacting *.googleapis.com / accounts.google.com. Rationale: Combines the article's OAuth-code-to-access-token exchange and Google-API access with the sideload host names confirmed in screenshot image1.jpeg; a renamed Bitdefender/VSTest/GoogleDesktop binary speaking directly to Google OAuth/Gmail APIs (work normally done only by the browser) is a strong, low-FP anomaly. Sentinel left empty because process-attributed network telemetry to these hosts is not available in standard Sentinel tables (would require Sysmon EID3 ingestion). Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/ • https://media.kasperskycontenthub.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/43/2026/06/16200713/image1.jpeg • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0228/
ATT&CKT1528 T1114.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuine Google Desktop legacy install (in Program Files) performing update/sync checks to googleapis.com
  • Bitdefender ConnectAgent telemetry/update traffic to a Google-hosted CDN (rare; mitigated by host-name + writable-path context)
  • Security testing of the binaries in a lab with live internet
  • A renamed-but-benign internal tool reusing one of these file names
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files (x86)"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating binary path/signer and verify it is the renamed sideload host rather than the genuine vendor product; pull the destination URLs and timing relative to any browser remote-debug launch. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the binary, and revoke the affected Google account's OAuth tokens/refresh tokens and active sessions; review Google Workspace audit logs for token grants and bulk message reads. 3) Hunt: enumerate other hosts where these binaries reach Google APIs, correlate with the log.dll sideload and KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp task, and check for mailbox data staged/exfiltrated.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("BDSubWiz.exe","bds.exe","VSTestVideoRecorder.exe","GoogleDesktop.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("oauth2.googleapis.com","accounts.google.com","www.googleapis.com","gmail.googleapis.com","googleapis.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("BDSubWiz.exe","bds.exe","VSTestVideoRecorder.exe","GoogleDesktop.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("oauth2.googleapis.com","accounts.google.com","www.googleapis.com","gmail.googleapis.com","googleapis.com")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: ToddyCat Sideload Host Contacting Google OAuth/Gmail API
id: e7b3c91d-5a42-4f8e-8c01-9d2f6a3b7e58
description: Detects a ToddyCat sideload-host binary (not a browser) making network connections to Google OAuth / Gmail API endpoints, indicating OAuth token exchange and remote mailbox access.
references:
  - https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/30
tags:
  - attack.t1528
  - attack.t1114.002
logsource:
  category: network_connection
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\BDSubWiz.exe'
      - '\bds.exe'
      - '\VSTestVideoRecorder.exe'
      - '\GoogleDesktop.exe'
    DestinationHostname|contains:
      - 'googleapis.com'
      - 'accounts.google.com'
      - 'oauth2.googleapis.com'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 (@Image:(*\\BDS.exe OR *\\bds.exe OR *\\BDSubWiz.exe OR *\\VSTestVideoRecorder.exe OR *\\GoogleDesktop.exe)) (@DestinationHostname:(*googleapis.com OR *accounts.google.com))
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/(googleapis\.com|accounts\.google\.com|oauth2\.googleapis\.com)/i | ContextImageFileName=/\\(BDSubWiz|bds|VSTestVideoRecorder|GoogleDesktop)\.exe$/i | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.process_name="BDSubWiz.exe" OR All_Traffic.process_name="bds.exe" OR All_Traffic.process_name="VSTestVideoRecorder.exe" OR All_Traffic.process_name="GoogleDesktop.exe") AND (All_Traffic.dest="*googleapis.com*" OR All_Traffic.dest="*accounts.google.com*") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.process_name All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.process_name="BDSubWiz.exe" OR All_Traffic.process_name="bds.exe" OR All_Traffic.process_name="VSTestVideoRecorder.exe" OR All_Traffic.process_name="GoogleDesktop.exe") AND (All_Traffic.dest="*googleapis.com*" OR All_Traffic.dest="*accounts.google.com*") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.process_name All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("1AB58838E5790EFB22F2D35AB98C0B7D", "A7D7D6C4C3F227F7117261C63B9E23A9", "3D3A621F852C42D97FD7260681E42508", "3432DD9AC0DF80EF86EB80BD080F839B", "22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE", "F61FBFB7AA1CD5DC8F70B055B51563E2", "F169D6D172DFB775895A5E2B1540C854", "9F5F2F0FB0A7F5AA9F16B9A7B6DAD89F", "28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1", "BAE82A15D1DBFB024617B9B56A8E5F66") or SHA1 in~ ("1AB58838E5790EFB22F2D35AB98C0B7D", "A7D7D6C4C3F227F7117261C63B9E23A9", "3D3A621F852C42D97FD7260681E42508", "3432DD9AC0DF80EF86EB80BD080F839B", "22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE", "F61FBFB7AA1CD5DC8F70B055B51563E2", "F169D6D172DFB775895A5E2B1540C854", "9F5F2F0FB0A7F5AA9F16B9A7B6DAD89F", "28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1", "BAE82A15D1DBFB024617B9B56A8E5F66") or MD5 in~ ("1AB58838E5790EFB22F2D35AB98C0B7D", "A7D7D6C4C3F227F7117261C63B9E23A9", "3D3A621F852C42D97FD7260681E42508", "3432DD9AC0DF80EF86EB80BD080F839B", "22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE", "F61FBFB7AA1CD5DC8F70B055B51563E2", "F169D6D172DFB775895A5E2B1540C854", "9F5F2F0FB0A7F5AA9F16B9A7B6DAD89F", "28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1", "BAE82A15D1DBFB024617B9B56A8E5F66")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("1AB58838E5790EFB22F2D35AB98C0B7D", "A7D7D6C4C3F227F7117261C63B9E23A9", "3D3A621F852C42D97FD7260681E42508", "3432DD9AC0DF80EF86EB80BD080F839B", "22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE", "F61FBFB7AA1CD5DC8F70B055B51563E2", "F169D6D172DFB775895A5E2B1540C854", "9F5F2F0FB0A7F5AA9F16B9A7B6DAD89F", "28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1", "BAE82A15D1DBFB024617B9B56A8E5F66") or SHA1 in~ ("1AB58838E5790EFB22F2D35AB98C0B7D", "A7D7D6C4C3F227F7117261C63B9E23A9", "3D3A621F852C42D97FD7260681E42508", "3432DD9AC0DF80EF86EB80BD080F839B", "22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE", "F61FBFB7AA1CD5DC8F70B055B51563E2", "F169D6D172DFB775895A5E2B1540C854", "9F5F2F0FB0A7F5AA9F16B9A7B6DAD89F", "28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1", "BAE82A15D1DBFB024617B9B56A8E5F66") or MD5 in~ ("1AB58838E5790EFB22F2D35AB98C0B7D", "A7D7D6C4C3F227F7117261C63B9E23A9", "3D3A621F852C42D97FD7260681E42508", "3432DD9AC0DF80EF86EB80BD080F839B", "22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE", "F61FBFB7AA1CD5DC8F70B055B51563E2", "F169D6D172DFB775895A5E2B1540C854", "9F5F2F0FB0A7F5AA9F16B9A7B6DAD89F", "28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1", "BAE82A15D1DBFB024617B9B56A8E5F66")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["1AB58838E5790EFB22F2D35AB98C0B7D", "A7D7D6C4C3F227F7117261C63B9E23A9", "3D3A621F852C42D97FD7260681E42508", "3432DD9AC0DF80EF86EB80BD080F839B", "22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE", "F61FBFB7AA1CD5DC8F70B055B51563E2", "F169D6D172DFB775895A5E2B1540C854", "9F5F2F0FB0A7F5AA9F16B9A7B6DAD89F", "28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1", "BAE82A15D1DBFB024617B9B56A8E5F66"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AirDrop and Quick Share Flaws Let Nearby Attackers Trigger Crashes and Bypass Checks

The Hacker News
2026-06-30 7 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Two researchers have found six security flaws in AirDrop and Quick Share, the wireless features that beam files between nearby devices with no cables or shared network. An attacker within wireless range, with just a laptop and no prior connection, can crash the sharing service on a Mac or iPhone set to receive from anyone, with no tap or prompt. The same research found Quick Share flaws that

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Google Quick Share for Windows (nearby_share.exe) spawning shell or LOLBin — UAF code execution · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Google Quick Share for Windows (nearby_share.exe) repeated crash/restart loop — UAF DoS · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Google Quick Share for Windows (nearby_share.exe) repeated crash/restart loop — UAF DoS AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for the Google Quick Share for Windows client (nearby_share.exe) crashing and restarting repeatedly on a single host, consistent with a nearby/same-LAN attacker repeatedly colliding two connections to trigger the use-after-free described in the CISPA research. A persistent tray app restarting 5+ times in 10 minutes is not normal lifecycle behaviour. Rationale: Uses the concrete Windows Quick Share client binary name (nearby_share.exe, publisher Google LLC) confirmed via the SpyShelter process DB, plus the article's claim of a crash triggered when two connections collide. A persistent tray app restarting 5+ times / crashing repeatedly is the observable footprint of the local UAF DoS. Cross-checked against: • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/30/apple-airdrop-google-samsung-quick-share-vulnerabilities/ • https://arxiv.org/html/2606.26967v1 • https://www.spyshelter.com/exe/google-llc-nearby_share-exe/
ATT&CKT1499.004 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine app instability after a Windows feature update or a corrupt Quick Share install causing repeated WER crashes
  • User repeatedly relaunching Quick Share manually from the system tray after it hangs on a large legitimate transfer
  • Quick Share auto-update mid-session restarting the client process several times
  • Driver/Wi-Fi adapter resets on the host destabilising the Bluetooth+Wi-Fi stack Quick Share depends on
  • Sysmon/Defender double-reporting the same process start during high event volume
Suppression filter
// Suppress benign updater-driven restarts
| where SampleFolder !has "\\Update\\" and SampleCompany has_any ("Google", "")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the host actually has Quick Share for Windows installed and pull the bin(10m) of nearby_share.exe starts / Application Error 1000 events; check whether the device was in a crowded shared space (airport/conference/office Wi-Fi) at crash time and whether CFG is enforced on the binary. 2) CONTAIN: Have the user close Quick Share and set visibility off 'Everyone' (out of receive mode); if the crash loop persists, isolate the host's Wi-Fi/Bluetooth or network-isolate and ensure the Google-patched Quick Share build is installed. 3) HUNT: Pivot to UC 'nearby_share.exe spawning a shell/LOLBin' on the same host/time window to rule out the crash being escalated to code execution, and check DeviceNetworkEvents for the inbound peer IP that preceded the crashes.
// Google Quick Share for Windows (nearby_share.exe) crash-restart loop — sustained proximity/LAN UAF DoS
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where FileName =~ "nearby_share.exe"
| summarize LaunchCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            SampleFolder = any(FolderPath), SampleCompany = any(ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName)
        by DeviceName, AccountName, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where LaunchCount >= 5   // >=5 (re)starts of the Quick Share tray app in 10 min = crash loop; normal lifecycle is 1 start per logon
| order by LastSeen desc
// Application Error (Event ID 1000) faulting on nearby_share.exe (Quick Share for Windows)
Event
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where EventLog == "Application"
| where Source == "Application Error" and EventID == 1000
| where RenderedDescription has "nearby_share.exe"
| summarize CrashCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            SampleDescription = any(RenderedDescription)
        by Computer, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where CrashCount >= 3   // >=3 app-error crashes of Quick Share in 10 min
| order by LastSeen desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\nearby_share.exe OR *\\Nearby_Share.exe OR *\\NEARBY_SHARE.EXE)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\nearby_share\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName], function=count())
| count >= 5
ENDPOINT

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| where count>=5
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

Google Quick Share for Windows (nearby_share.exe) spawning shell or LOLBin — UAF code execution AIExploitation High
Hunts for the Quick Share for Windows client (nearby_share.exe) spawning a command shell, scripting host, or download-capable LOLBin as a child. The CISPA research notes the Windows use-after-free is plausibly exploitable for code execution because Control Flow Guard is disabled in the app; nearby_share.exe legitimately spawns no such children, so any is high-fidelity. Rationale: Grounded in the article's specific claim that the Windows Quick Share UAF is plausibly exploitable for code execution (CFG off). Uses the concrete parent binary nearby_share.exe; this tray app has no legitimate reason to spawn cmd/powershell/mshta/rundll32 etc., making the parent->child pair high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/30/apple-airdrop-google-samsung-quick-share-vulnerabilities/ • https://arxiv.org/html/2606.26967v1 • https://www.spyshelter.com/exe/google-llc-nearby_share-exe/
ATT&CKT1203 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Quick Share updater logic shelling out to a maintenance/cleanup script during an in-place upgrade
  • Enterprise software-management agent injecting a child process under nearby_share.exe for inventory
  • Security tooling (EDR/DLP) reparenting or hollowing nearby_share.exe causing an apparent child spawn
  • An IT helpdesk troubleshooting script launched while Quick Share happened to be the foreground process (rare reparent)
Suppression filter
// Drop known updater path if it legitimately invokes cmd in your environment
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\Quick Share\\Update\\"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Inspect the child ProcessCommandLine and SHA256 — decode any encoded/obfuscated args, check the child's network connections and file writes, and confirm whether a Quick Share crash (UC1) or an inbound peer connection immediately preceded this on the same host. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, kill the child process tree, and capture nearby_share.exe memory; block the child binary hash if attacker-supplied. 3) HUNT: Sweep the fleet for the same parent->child pair, pivot on the child's C2 destinations across DeviceNetworkEvents, and verify all endpoints run Google's patched Quick Share build.
// nearby_share.exe (Quick Share for Windows) spawning a shell/LOLBin child — possible UAF -> code execution
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "nearby_share.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
// 4688: nearby_share.exe spawning shell/LOLBin
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\nearby_share.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\mshta.exe","\\rundll32.exe","\\regsvr32.exe","\\bitsadmin.exe","\\certutil.exe","\\curl.exe","\\wget.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 7c2e9b14-0a3d-4f86-9b21-3f7c5d61ea48
status: experimental
description: Detects the Quick Share for Windows client spawning a command shell, scripting host, or download-capable LOLBin, consistent with exploitation of the disclosed use-after-free (CFG disabled in the app).
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/airdrop-and-quick-share-flaws-let.html
  - https://arxiv.org/html/2606.26967v1
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/30
tags:
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1203
  - attack.t1059
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    ParentImage|endswith: '\nearby_share.exe'
    Image|endswith:
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
      - '\mshta.exe'
      - '\rundll32.exe'
      - '\regsvr32.exe'
      - '\bitsadmin.exe'
      - '\certutil.exe'
      - '\curl.exe'
      - '\wget.exe'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\nearby_share.exe OR *\\Nearby_Share.exe OR *\\NEARBY_SHARE.EXE) @Image:(*\\cmd.exe OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe OR *\\wscript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\mshta.exe OR *\\rundll32.exe OR *\\regsvr32.exe OR *\\bitsadmin.exe OR *\\certutil.exe OR *\\curl.exe OR *\\wget.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/nearby_share\.exe/i
| ImageFileName=/\\(cmd|powershell|pwsh|wscript|cscript|mshta|rundll32|regsvr32|bitsadmin|certutil|curl|wget)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="nearby_share.exe" AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe") by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="nearby_share.exe" AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe") by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - lastTime
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

2026-06-30 6 use cases 5 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Convince an AI browser that it is playing a game, and it can hand over your login details. That is the finding behind&nbsp;BioShocking, a technique from security firm LayerX that tricked six AI browsers and assistants into copying a user's credentials and sending them to an attacker. The targets included OpenAI's ChatGPT Atlas, Perplexity's Comet, and Anthropic's Claude browser extension. An

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",

Progress Kemp LoadMaster Flaw Could Let Attackers Run Root Commands Pre-Auth

The Hacker News
2026-06-30 12 use cases 5 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A critical vulnerability in Progress Kemp LoadMaster can let an unauthenticated attacker execute arbitrary commands as root on the appliance by sending a crafted request to its API. The flaw, tracked as&nbsp;CVE-2026-8037, carries a CVSS score of&nbsp;9.8 according to ZDI. A patch is available. If you run LoadMaster with the API enabled, update now. Progress&nbsp;published its advisory on June

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Kemp LoadMaster CVE-2026-33691 WAF bypass via whitespace-padded upload filename extension · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Kemp LoadMaster CVE-2026-8037 pre-auth RCE via /accessv2 heap-overflow command injection · [LLM] Root command execution on Kemp LoadMaster appliance following /accessv2 exploitation · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.

Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Kemp LoadMaster CVE-2026-8037 pre-auth RCE via /accessv2 heap-overflow command injection AIExploitation High
Hunts the watchTowr PoC payload shape for CVE-2026-8037: an unauthenticated POST to the LoadMaster /accessv2 API endpoint whose JSON body sprays many extra keys (g0..g60) each carrying a '; <cmd> # shell-injection string plus a 16-byte 'AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA' padding prefix and an apiuser value of four single quotes. This is the exact initial-access signature against an internet-facing appliance, not a generic web-attack template. Rationale: Grounded on the exact watchTowr PoC strings cross-checked from the labs.watchtowr.com write-up: endpoint /accessv2, the 16-byte 'AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA' heap-padding prefix, the '; cat /etc/passwd # injection, the g0..g60 key spray, and apiuser ''''. Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch empty because LoadMaster is a closed Kemp appliance not enrolled in EDR/XDR or AWS; the request body lives in WAF/proxy CEF or the appliance's own syslog. Cross-checked against: • https://labs.watchtowr.com/enterprise-tech-in-shell-out-progress-kemp-loadmaster-uninitialized-heap-to-pre-auth-rce-cve-2026-8037/ • https://community.progress.com/s/article/LoadMaster-Critical-Security-Bulletin-June-2026-CVE-2026-8037-CVE-2026-33691 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/progress-kemp-loadmaster-flaw-could-let.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized penetration test or watchTowr 'Detection Artefact' validation firing the same payload
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys) sending CVE-2026-8037 check payloads to /accessv2
  • Internal red-team exercises replaying the public PoC
  • WAF in blocking mode logging the attempt as 'denied' (true positive but already mitigated)
  • Legitimate high-volume API credential validation traffic tripping the 20-POST burst threshold during automation onboarding
Suppression filter
| where DeviceAction != "blocked" and DeviceAction != "denied" and SourceIP !in ("<authorized_scanner_ips_reference_table>")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the matching CommonSecurityLog rows; confirm the source IP is external/untrusted and the body contains the injection markers (g0..g60 spray, '; ... #, /etc/passwd). Check whether the WAF action was 'allowed' vs 'blocked'. 2) CONTAIN: If allowed, treat the LoadMaster as compromised at root — isolate it from the management network, block the source IP at the edge, and disable the LoadMaster API if not strictly required (per advisory). Begin emergency patch to GA v7.2.63.2 / LTSF v7.2.54.18. 3) HUNT: Pivot to the appliance's syslog (UC: root command execution) for shell activity (/etc/passwd reads, reverse shells), review LoadMaster config and SSH authorized_keys for persistence, and scope all source IPs that hit /accessv2 with these markers across the full retention window.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL has "/accessv2"
| where Message has_any ("'; cat /etc/passwd #", "AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA", "/etc/passwd", "\"g60\"", "\"apiuser\":\"''''\"")
   or RequestContext has_any ("'; cat /etc/passwd #", "AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA", "/etc/passwd")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourcePort, DestinationIP, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Progress Kemp LoadMaster CVE-2026-8037 Pre-Auth RCE Exploitation Attempt
id: 7e2b1c4a-9d3e-4f51-bc62-3a8f0d5e91aa
status: experimental
description: Detects exploitation attempts against the Kemp LoadMaster /accessv2 endpoint using the watchTowr CVE-2026-8037 uninitialized-heap command-injection payload pattern (16-byte A padding prefix plus a '; <cmd> # injection).

    condition: selection_endpoint and selection_payload

Root command execution on Kemp LoadMaster appliance following /accessv2 exploitation AIExploitation Medium
Execution-phase confirmation for CVE-2026-8037: the injected command runs as root on the LoadMaster appliance. Hunts the appliance's forwarded syslog for shell-command execution indicators (/etc/passwd reads, /bin/sh -c, reverse-shell /dev/tcp/ or bash -i) originating from a host named like a LoadMaster, which should never legitimately spawn arbitrary shells. Rationale: Targets the article's core claim that the command 'runs as root' on the appliance. A load balancer spawning /bin/sh, reading /etc/passwd, or opening a /dev/tcp reverse shell is never legitimate, making these high-fidelity post-exploitation indicators. Empty Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch: the appliance cannot host an EDR agent — only its remote syslog is observable. Hunting tier because it depends on the appliance being configured to forward syslog and named per convention. Cross-checked against: • https://labs.watchtowr.com/enterprise-tech-in-shell-out-progress-kemp-loadmaster-uninitialized-heap-to-pre-auth-rce-cve-2026-8037/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/progress-kemp-loadmaster-flaw-could-let.html
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Kemp support/diagnostic sessions where an admin legitimately opens a root shell for troubleshooting
  • Firmware update or backup routines that touch /etc/passwd or spawn shell helpers
  • Authorized configuration scripts run by the appliance's own automation
  • Penetration test PoC replay reading /etc/passwd
  • Syslog from a non-appliance host that happens to match the 'kemp'/'loadmaster' name substring
Suppression filter
| where SyslogMessage !has "kemp-support" and SeverityLevel != "debug"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the source host is genuinely the LoadMaster appliance and that the shell activity has no matching authorized admin/maintenance window; correlate the timestamp against /accessv2 POST hits (UC1) within the preceding minutes. 2) CONTAIN: If unexplained, isolate the appliance from management and production networks, capture a config/state snapshot for forensics, and rotate any credentials/keys stored on or reachable from the appliance. 3) HUNT: Enumerate persistence — SSH authorized_keys under /root, cron/systemd entries, modified LoadMaster config — and review egress firewall logs for outbound connections initiated by the appliance IP (reverse shell / tooling download).
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Computer has_any ("loadmaster", "lmos", "kemp") or HostName has_any ("loadmaster", "lmos", "kemp")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("/etc/passwd", "/dev/tcp/", "bash -i", "/bin/sh -c", "/bin/bash -c", "; cat ", "| sh")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostName, Facility, SeverityLevel, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog (@host.name:(*loadmaster* OR *LoadMaster* OR *lmos* OR *kemp* OR *Kemp*)) AND ("/etc/passwd" OR "/dev/tcp/" OR "bash -i" OR "/bin/sh -c" OR "/bin/bash -c")
WEB
index=* sourcetype=syslog (host=*loadmaster* OR host=*lmos* OR host=*kemp*) ("/etc/passwd" OR "/dev/tcp/" OR "bash -i" OR "/bin/sh -c" OR "/bin/bash -c")
| table _time host process syslog_message
| sort - _time
| comment("LoadMaster forwards to a non-CIM syslog sourcetype; raw search. Scope host to your appliance naming convention.")
Kemp LoadMaster CVE-2026-33691 WAF bypass via whitespace-padded upload filename extension AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the second patched flaw in the same advisory: a WAF/upload extension-check bypass where whitespace padding around a filename extension (e.g. evil.php<space> or evil .php / %20.php) slips a disallowed file type past the filter. Detects upload requests to LoadMaster whose filename contains whitespace adjacent to an executable/script extension. Rationale: Grounded on the advisory's description of CVE-2026-33691 — 'whitespace padding in filenames could circumvent file upload extension checks.' Matches whitespace immediately adjacent to a script/executable extension in the upload filename or URL-encoded path, a pattern legitimate uploads almost never produce. Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch empty: appliance upload telemetry lives only in the front-end WAF/proxy, not in endpoint EDR or AWS. Cross-checked against: • https://community.progress.com/s/article/LoadMaster-Critical-Security-Bulletin-June-2026-CVE-2026-8037-CVE-2026-33691 • https://securityonline.info/kemp-loadmaster-vulnerabilities-waf-bypass-os-injection/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/progress-kemp-loadmaster-flaw-could-let.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1036.008
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user uploading a legitimately named file that happens to contain a trailing space before a known extension
  • Document-management workflows that rename files with padded extensions
  • Automated tooling that URL-encodes spaces (%20) in legitimate filenames
  • Security scanner testing upload filters with whitespace mutation payloads
  • Double-extension business files (e.g. report.tar .gz) tripping the regex
Suppression filter
| where FileName !endswith " .gz" and FileName !endswith " .bz2" and SourceIP !in ("<authorized_scanner_ips_reference_table>")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Inspect the captured filename and upload endpoint; confirm the whitespace is adjacent to an executable/script extension (.php/.cgi/.sh) rather than a benign document type, and identify the resulting stored path. 2) CONTAIN: If a script/webshell-capable file was accepted, quarantine it on the appliance, block the source IP, and confirm the appliance is patched to GA v7.2.63.2 / LTSF v7.2.54.18. 3) HUNT: Search appliance syslog for subsequent execution of the uploaded path, review web logs for requests back to the uploaded filename (webshell interaction), and scope all sources that submitted whitespace-padded upload filenames.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod =~ "POST" or RequestMethod =~ "PUT" or isempty(RequestMethod)
| where FileName matches regex @"(?i)\s+\.(php|cgi|sh|pl|jsp|asp|aspx|exe)\b"
    or FileName matches regex @"(?i)\.(php|cgi|sh|pl|jsp|asp|aspx|exe)\s+$"
    or RequestURL has_any ("%20.php", "%20.cgi", "%20.sh", ".php%20", ".cgi%20")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, RequestURL, RequestMethod, FileName, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

         from datamodel=Email.All_Email

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High

ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001

DeviceProcessEvents

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
