OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Gamaredon Expands Ukraine Attacks with New Malware and Cloud Service Abuse

The Hacker News
2026-06-29 16 use cases 6 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

A Russian advanced persistent threat (APT) group has continued to evolve and expand its malware arsenal as part of its ongoing cyber onslaught against Ukraine throughout 2025. Slovakian cybersecurity company ESET said it observed 35 distinct spear-phishing campaigns mounted by Gamaredon against new targets, with most of them taking place in the second half of the year. Gamaredon CVE-2025-8088 WinRAR ADS path traversal dropping payload into Startup folder AIInstallation High
Hunts the Gamaredon-specific abuse of WinRAR path traversal (CVE-2025-8088, NTFS Alternate Data Stream traversal) to write its HTA downloader (or LNK/VBS) directly into the user's Startup folder during archive extraction, granting login persistence. Pivots on an archive tool writing an auto-executing file type outside the intended extraction directory. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete chain: WinRAR (CVE-2025-8088) writing the HTA downloader into the Windows Startup folder for next-login persistence. An archive extractor creating an auto-run file outside its own folder is the direct ADS-traversal artifact. Cross-checked ESET and NVD. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/gamaredon-2025-leveraging-tunnels-workers-dead-drops-new-alliances/ • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2025-8088 • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/exploiting-critical-winrar-vulnerability
ATT&CKT1203 T1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user legitimately extracting a portable app archive that places a real .exe/.lnk into Startup intentionally
  • Software installers shipped as RAR/7z self-extractors that add a legitimate startup entry
  • explorer.exe creating shortcuts in Startup when a user pins an app to run at login
  • Backup/sync tools restoring a Startup folder from an archive
  • IT-packaged onboarding archives that seed approved startup utilities
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "explorer.exe" and FileName endswith ".lnk" and InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm WinRAR/Rar version on the host via DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory — versions <7.13 are vulnerable; pull the dropped file's SHA256 and detonate/scan it; note if extension is .hta/.lnk. 2) Contain: isolate the host before next login (the Startup file auto-executes on logon), delete the Startup payload, and force WinRAR upgrade to 7.13+. 3) Hunt: search the same user/host for the source archive (email or USB origin), mshta.exe execution of the dropped HTA, and outbound traffic to dead-drop resolver domains.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FolderPath has @"\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("winrar.exe","rar.exe","unrar.exe","7zFM.exe","explorer.exe")
| where FileName endswith ".hta" or FileName endswith ".lnk" or FileName endswith ".vbs" or FileName endswith ".exe" or FileName endswith ".cmd" or FileName endswith ".js"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("winrar.exe","rar.exe","unrar.exe","7zFM.exe","explorer.exe")
| where TargetFileName endswith ".hta" or TargetFileName endswith ".lnk" or TargetFileName endswith ".vbs" or TargetFileName endswith ".exe" or TargetFileName endswith ".cmd"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 Path Traversal Writing Autostart Payload to Startup Folder
id: 5f3c2a7e-9b41-4d8c-bb2e-7a1d6e9f0c12
description: Detects an archive utility writing an auto-executing file type into the user Startup folder, consistent with Gamaredon abuse of WinRAR ADS path traversal (CVE-2025-8088) for login persistence.
references:
  - https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/gamaredon-2025-leveraging-tunnels-workers-dead-drops-new-alliances/
  - https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2025-8088
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/29
tags:
  - attack.t1203
  - attack.t1547.001
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\winrar.exe'
      - '\rar.exe'
      - '\unrar.exe'
      - '\7zFM.exe'
    TargetFilename|contains: '\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\'
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '.hta'
      - '.lnk'
      - '.vbs'
      - '.exe'
      - '.cmd'
      - '.js'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @Image:(*\\WinRAR.exe OR *\\winrar.exe OR *\\Rar.exe OR *\\rar.exe OR *\\UnRAR.exe OR *\\7zFM.exe) @TargetFilename:(*\\Startup\\* OR *\\startup\\*) @TargetFilename:(*.hta OR *.lnk OR *.vbs OR *.exe OR *.cmd OR *.js)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| ContextImageFileName=/\\(winrar|rar|unrar|7zfm)\.exe$/i
| TargetFileName=/\\Microsoft\\Windows\\Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup\\/i
| TargetFileName=/\.(hta|lnk|vbs|exe|cmd|js)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.action=created Filesystem.file_path="*\\Microsoft\\Windows\\Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup\\*" (Filesystem.file_name="*.hta" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.lnk" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.vbs" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.exe" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.cmd" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.js") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | search process_name IN ("winrar.exe","rar.exe","unrar.exe","7zFM.exe","explorer.exe","WinRAR.exe") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.action=created Filesystem.file_path="*\\Microsoft\\Windows\\Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup\\*" (Filesystem.file_name="*.hta" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.lnk" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.vbs" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.exe" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.cmd" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.js") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | search process_name IN ("winrar.exe","rar.exe","unrar.exe","7zFM.exe","explorer.exe","WinRAR.exe") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Gamaredon spear-phishing delivery via HTML-smuggling XHTML or archive attachment AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the Gamaredon initial-access vector: inbound spear-phishing mail delivering archive attachments (RAR/ZIP/7z) or XHTML/HTM files that use HTML smuggling to reconstruct a malicious HTA downloader client-side. Surfaces delivered messages carrying these attachment types so analysts can pivot to recipient-host execution. Rationale: Targets the article's stated delivery: 'archive attachments or XHTML files that employ HTML smuggling' to deliver HTA downloaders. The XHTML/HTM attachment type is the high-signal HTML-smuggling marker; archive types cover the alternate path. Sentinel/Falcon/Datadog left empty as inbound mail-attachment telemetry lives only in Defender for O365 (EmailAttachmentInfo) in this tenant. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/gamaredon-2025-leveraging-tunnels-workers-dead-drops-new-alliances/ • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/26/f/old-winrar-flaw-fuels-attacks-on-ukraine.html
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1027.006
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate business RAR/ZIP/7z attachments (invoices, reports) from known partners
  • Marketing or newsletter mail with HTML/HTM body parts saved as attachments
  • Internal-to-external auto-forwarded archives misclassified as inbound
  • Developers exchanging .htm/.xhtml documentation files
  • Compressed log bundles sent to support inboxes
Response runbook
1) Triage: detonate the attachment SHA256 in a sandbox; for XHTML/HTM open it to confirm embedded base64 blob + JS Blob/anchor-download (HTML smuggling) reconstructing an HTA. 2) Contain: quarantine/soft-delete the message tenant-wide via EmailPostDeliveryEvents purge, block the sender domain, and check whether any recipient already opened it. 3) Hunt: on each recipient host, look for an HTA written to Temp/Startup and subsequent mshta.exe execution; check DeviceFileEvents for the smuggled HTA file write.
let SuspectExt = dynamic(["rar","zip","7z","xhtml","htm","html","hta"]);
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where DeliveryAction in ("Delivered","DeliveredAsSpam")
| join kind=inner (
    EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | extend Ext = tolower(tostring(split(FileName, ".")[-1]))
    | where Ext in (SuspectExt)
    | project NetworkMessageId, AttachmentName = FileName, Ext, FileType, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, AttachmentName, Ext, AttachmentSHA256, DeliveryAction
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
let SuspectExt = dynamic(["rar","zip","7z","xhtml","htm","html","hta"]);
EmailEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where DeliveryAction in ("Delivered","DeliveredAsSpam")
| join kind=inner (
    EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | extend Ext = tolower(tostring(split(FileName, ".")[-1]))
    | where Ext in (SuspectExt)
    | project NetworkMessageId, AttachmentName = FileName, Ext, FileType, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| project TimeGenerated, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, AttachmentName, Ext, AttachmentSHA256, DeliveryAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc
Gamaredon HTA downloader executed via mshta.exe from Startup/Temp AIExploitation High
Hunts execution of the Gamaredon HTA downloader by mshta.exe pointing at an .hta in the Startup, Temp, AppData or Public path (the auto-run persistence payload dropped via WinRAR/HTML smuggling), or mshta spawned by explorer/winrar/script hosts. This is the execution pivot that turns delivery+persistence into payload retrieval (e.g. PteroSand). Rationale: mshta.exe running a .hta out of Startup/Temp/AppData (or launched by explorer.exe on login, or by winrar.exe right after extraction) is the precise Gamaredon HTA-downloader execution step that drops PteroSand. Path + parent constraints keep it off generic mshta noise. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/gamaredon-2025-leveraging-tunnels-workers-dead-drops-new-alliances/ • https://gbhackers.com/winrar-cve-2025-8088-exploited/
ATT&CKT1218.005 T1059.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy line-of-business apps that legitimately launch HTA UIs from AppData
  • Enterprise software using mshta for installer/help dialogs out of Temp
  • Admin scripts wrapping mshta for one-off automation
  • RMM/management agents invoking mshta from ProgramData
  • Browser/email clients caching an .htm to Temp opened by mshta during a benign workflow
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has @"\ProgramData\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full mshta command line and the HTA file contents/SHA256; confirm whether the HTA path is the Startup folder (persistence) and decode any inline javascript:/vbscript:. 2) Contain: kill the mshta process tree, isolate the host, and remove the HTA from Startup so it does not re-trigger on logon. 3) Hunt: follow the child processes (powershell.exe/wscript.exe) and outbound connections to dead-drop resolver services; pivot on the same SHA256 across the fleet and to the originating archive/email.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "mshta.exe"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (".hta", "javascript:", "vbscript:")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\Startup\", @"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", @"\Public\", @"\ProgramData\")
    or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","winrar.exe","rar.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\mshta.exe"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| where CommandLine has_any (".hta", "javascript:", "vbscript:")
| where CommandLine has_any (@"\Startup\", @"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", @"\Public\", @"\ProgramData\")
    or ParentProcessName endswith "\\explorer.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\winrar.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\wscript.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\cscript.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Gamaredon PowerShell/HTA tools fetching C2 via dead-drop resolver cloud services AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the Gamaredon C2-resolution behaviour: scripting hosts (PowerShell, mshta, wscript, cscript, rundll32) reaching legitimate paste/blog/cloud-storage services used as dead-drop resolvers and payload hosts — Telegra.ph (PteroOdd), GoFile (PteroEffigy), Teletype, Rentry.co, Write.as, Paste.ee, Dropbox, Wasabi, Tebi. These services front the real C2 hidden behind tunnels/workers. Rationale: The article names the exact dead-drop resolver set (Telegra.ph→PteroOdd, GoFile→PteroEffigy, plus Teletype/Rentry/Write.as/Paste.ee/Dropbox/Wasabi/Tebi). A scripting host — not a browser — reaching these from a non-machine account is the high-fidelity C2-resolution signal. Sentinel uses DnsEvents (no per-process filter available on that table, so it is broader; pair with endpoint process telemetry). Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/gamaredon-2025-leveraging-tunnels-workers-dead-drops-new-alliances/ • https://www.technadu.com/gamaredon-2025-new-tools-turla-alliance-cloud-exfiltration/629948/
ATT&CKT1102.001 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers/SREs running PowerShell scripts that legitimately pull artifacts from Dropbox or Wasabi/Tebi S3-compatible buckets
  • Automation using curl-via-powershell to fetch Gists/pastes for tooling
  • rundll32 in a benign app making telemetry calls that resolve a shared CDN
  • Technical writers' scripts posting to Dev.to/Telegra.ph APIs
  • Backup jobs reaching Wasabi/Dropbox object storage from scripted tasks
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("choco","scoop","winget","\\Jenkins\\","azure-pipelines") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full InitiatingProcessCommandLine — confirm the script is downloading/parsing a paste (Invoke-WebRequest/DownloadString to telegra.ph/gofile) rather than a sanctioned dev workflow; extract any second-stage URL the dead drop returns. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the script process, and block the resolved C2 IP/tunnel domain at the proxy/firewall. 3) Hunt: decode the dead-drop response for the real C2 (often behind *.workers.dev / DDNS / tunnels), and sweep the fleet for the same scripting-host→dead-drop pattern and for the upstream HTA/Startup persistence.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","rundll32.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("telegra.ph","teletype.in","rentry.co","write.as","gofile.io","paste.ee","nopaste.net","dev.to","mastodon.social","tebi.io","wasabisys.com","dropbox.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has_any ("telegra.ph","teletype.in","rentry.co","write.as","gofile.io","paste.ee","nopaste.net","tebi.io","wasabisys.com","dropbox.com")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, QueryTypeName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Gamaredon PteroLNK/PteroSetup weaponizing USB and network drives with LNK files AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the Gamaredon worming behaviour: a scripting host (wscript/cscript/powershell/mshta) creating malicious .lnk files on removable or mapped network drives (PteroLNK) to spread to other users and hosts. Scopes to file writes outside the system drive to surface USB/network-drive infection. Rationale: Targets PteroLNK/PteroSetup behaviour the article describes: infecting USB and network drives with malicious LNK files via script weaponizers. A script host writing .lnk files off the system drive (removable/mapped) is a rare, high-signal worming artifact; the count pivot catches bulk drive-wide seeding. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/gamaredon-2025-leveraging-tunnels-workers-dead-drops-new-alliances/ • https://web-assets.esetstatic.com/wls/en/papers/white-papers/gamaredon-in-2025.pdf
ATT&CKT1091 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Login scripts (cscript/wscript) deploying shortcut files to mapped home/share drives
  • Software deployment scripts creating app shortcuts on network shares
  • PowerShell DSC/GPO tooling provisioning Start Menu shortcuts to redirected folders
  • Backup or roaming-profile sync writing .lnk files to a network profile path
  • Admin maintenance scripts staging shortcuts on a USB toolkit drive
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\NETLOGON\\","\\SYSVOL\\","logon.vbs","Deploy-Application"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect one created .lnk target/arguments — Gamaredon LNKs invoke mshta/powershell to fetch a downloader; confirm the drive type (removable vs mapped) and the seeding script's command line. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block/remove the malicious LNKs from the affected share, and identify other hosts that mounted the same removable/network drive. 3) Hunt: search for the source weaponizer script (VBScript/PowerShell) and for execution of the dropped LNKs elsewhere, plus the downloader callbacks to dead-drop resolver services.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName endswith ".lnk"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where not(FolderPath startswith "C:\\")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize LnkCount = count(), Paths = make_set(FolderPath, 20), arg_min(Timestamp, *) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by LnkCount desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName endswith ".lnk"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where not(TargetFilePath startswith "C:\\")
| summarize LnkCount = count(), Paths = make_set(TargetFilePath, 20), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActorUsername
| order by LnkCount desc
title: Scripting Host Writing LNK Files to Non-System Drive (Gamaredon PteroLNK)
id: e9b2c5a1-7d34-4f60-8c19-3a6e1b9d4f72
description: Detects wscript/cscript/powershell/mshta creating .lnk files outside the system drive, consistent with Gamaredon PteroLNK weaponizing USB and network drives.
references:

detection:

level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @Image:(*\\wscript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\mshta.exe) @TargetFilename:(*.lnk) -@TargetFilename:C\:\\*
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| ContextImageFileName=/\\(wscript|cscript|powershell|pwsh|mshta)\.exe$/i
| TargetFileName=/\.lnk$/i
| NOT (TargetFileName=/^C:\\/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
| count > 1

| tstats summariesonly=false count values(Filesystem.file_path) as paths min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.action=created Filesystem.file_name="*.lnk" Filesystem.process_name IN ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe") NOT Filesystem.file_path="C:\\*" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where count > 1 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent

                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-8088")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",

                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time

| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

The Gentlemen network sniffing via netsh trace capture redirected to ADMIN$ share AIReconnaissance High
Hunts The Gentlemen's reconnaissance technique of running netsh trace packet capture and writing the .etl output across the network to a remote host's ADMIN$ share. The redirect of a netsh trace start/stop session to \\<ip>\ADMIN$\ is highly specific to this actor's credential-harvesting-from-the-wire workflow. Rationale: Built from the article's exact commands 'netsh trace start capture=yes report=no filemode=circular overwrite=yes maxSize=4 > \\<target IP>\ADMIN$\{RANDOM}' and the matching 'netsh trace stop' redirect. netsh trace + ADMIN$ redirect is rare in benign admin use, making this high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/i/unmasking-the-gentlemen-ransomware.html • https://www.huntress.com/blog/the-gentlemen-ransomware-defense-evasion-ttps
ATT&CKT1040 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Network engineer running netsh trace for legitimate troubleshooting and saving to a local file (no ADMIN$ redirect)
  • Endpoint support tooling that captures ETL traces locally
  • Microsoft support diagnostic scripts (TSS toolkit) invoking netsh trace
  • Vendor performance-monitoring agents starting circular ETW captures
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\TSS\\", "TSSv2") and AccountName endswith "admin")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the redirect target — a \\<remote-ip>\ADMIN$ path means cross-host write, not local troubleshooting. Identify the executing account and whether it is an admin/service account that does not normally run netsh. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the source host, reset the credentials of the executing account, and pull the dropped .etl from the target ADMIN$ share for analysis (it may contain cleartext creds). 3) HUNT: Search for SharpADWS/NetScan/Advanced IP Scanner activity, the deploy_gpo.ps1 script, and connections to 81.177.215.15:9443 on the same hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "netsh" and ProcessCommandLine has "trace"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("capture=yes", @"\ADMIN$\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| where CommandLine has "netsh" and CommandLine has "trace"
| where CommandLine has_any ("capture=yes", "\\ADMIN$\\")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

The Gentlemen Go backdoor C2 beacon to 81.177.215.15 on TCP/9443 AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any host establishing an outbound connection to the confirmed Gentlemen Go-backdoor C2 IP 81.177.215.15 on port 9443, the Yamux-multiplexed persistent channel used for remote command execution and SOCKS proxying. Single confirmed C2 indicator deployed a day before ransomware. Rationale: Uses the article's explicit C2 endpoint 81.177.215.15:9443 for the Yamux-based Go backdoor. A hardcoded malicious IP+port is a high-confidence, near-zero-FP network IOC. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/28/the-gentlemen-ransomware-dissecting-a-self-propagating-go-encryptor/ • https://s2w.inc/en/resource/detail/1053
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researchers/sandbox detonating the sample from corporate ranges
  • Threat-intel scanning or Shodan-style internet measurement hitting the IP
  • Reused VPS IP later assigned to a benign service (validate against current TI reputation)
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the InitiatingProcess making the connection — a Go binary in an unusual path (Temp/Public/AppData) deployed ~1 day prior is the backdoor. Capture its SHA256 against the article's hash list. 2) CONTAIN: Network-isolate the host, block 81.177.215.15 at the perimeter, and kill/quarantine the implant binary. 3) HUNT: Look for WMI query 'SELECT UUID FROM Win32_ComputerSystemProduct', cmd.exe /c children of the implant (operator command 'c'), SOCKS proxy listeners, and expect ransomware staging within ~24h.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "81.177.215.15" and RemotePort == 9443
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "81.177.215.15" and DstPortNumber == 9443
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

The Gentlemen BYOVD vulnerable driver drop/load (EDR-killer drivers) AIInstallation High
Hunts for the specific vulnerable kernel drivers The Gentlemen abuse in their BYOVD/GentleKiller workflow to terminate security products. Matches on the named .sys files being written or loaded, e.g. biontdrv.sys, wamsdk.sys, ProcessMonitorDriver.sys. Rationale: Driver names taken verbatim from the article's vulnerable-driver table (Safetica, WatchDog, Paragon biontdrv, inpoutx64, etc.). ESET's GentleKiller research corroborates these as the actor's BYOVD arsenal. Medium FP because inpoutx64.sys/biontdrv.sys also appear in legitimate software. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/killing-me-gently-inside-gentlemens-edr-killer-framework/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/gentlemen-ransomware-uses-multiple-edr-killers-to-disable-defenses/
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • inpoutx64.sys loaded by legitimate RGB-lighting/overclocking utilities
  • biontdrv.sys present from a genuine Paragon Partition Manager install
  • gamedriverx64.sys from a legitimately installed game with anti-cheat
  • Security product (Safetica) itself loading ProcessMonitorDriver.sys in an authorized deployment
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Program Files\" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe","paragon.exe")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Check the signing status and the parent process that wrote/loaded the driver — a driver dropped to a non-standard path by a non-installer process is malicious; a vendor MSI installer is likely benign. Confirm whether the matching legitimate product is actually installed. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, stop the driver service, and quarantine the .sys + the loading process; verify EDR/AV agents are still running. 3) HUNT: Correlate with Set-MpPreference tampering, OpenArk64/PowerRun.exe execution, and the 81.177.215.15 C2 on the same host to confirm Gentlemen activity.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("ProcessMonitorDriver.sys","wamsdk.sys","gamedriverx64.sys","biontdrv.sys","inpoutx64.sys","wsftprm.sys","Havoc.sys")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("ProcessMonitorDriver.sys","wamsdk.sys","gamedriverx64.sys","biontdrv.sys","inpoutx64.sys","wsftprm.sys","Havoc.sys")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

The Gentlemen impair defenses via Set-MpPreference exclusions and AV-removal tooling AIInstallation High
Detects The Gentlemen's defense-evasion step that disables Defender real-time/CFA protection, adds whole-drive exclusions via Set-MpPreference/Add-MpPreference, and runs known AV-removal utilities (kavrmvr.exe, OpenArk64, PowerRun.exe, Allpatch2.exe). Pairs the Go-implant PowerShell cmdlets with named tampering binaries. Rationale: Combines the article's verbatim Go-implant cmdlets (Set-MpPreference -DisableRealtimeMonitoring, -EnableControlledFolderAccess Disabled, Add-MpPreference -ExclusionProcess/-ExclusionPath 'C:\') with named tools kavrmvr.exe (Kaspersky uninstaller) and OpenArk64; PowerRun.exe/Allpatch2.exe added from corroborating Trend Micro reporting on the same actor. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/i/unmasking-the-gentlemen-ransomware.html • https://www.huntress.com/blog/the-gentlemen-ransomware-defense-evasion-ttps
ATT&CKT1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT admin legitimately adding a Defender exclusion for a line-of-business app (single ExclusionPath, not C:\)
  • Sanctioned migration off Kaspersky running kavrmvr.exe with change-ticket approval
  • Performance team disabling Real-Time Monitoring temporarily during a benchmark
  • Software packaging/SCCM scripts setting exclusions for an installer
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has "ExclusionPath" and ProcessCommandLine !has @"'C:\'" and ProcessCommandLine !has "DisableRealtimeMonitoring" and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ccmexec.exe","tiworker.exe"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Inspect the exclusion scope — a whole-drive 'C:\' exclusion or DisableRealtimeMonitoring chained with ExclusionProcess is malicious; a narrow app path may be benign. Identify the parent process (Go implant / cmd.exe /c). 2) CONTAIN: Re-enable Defender real-time protection and CFA, remove rogue exclusions, isolate the host, and reset the executing account. 3) HUNT: Pivot to BYOVD driver loads, registry Defender-policy keys, deploy_gpo.ps1, and the 81.177.215.15 C2 to scope the intrusion.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName in~ ("kavrmvr.exe","OpenArk64.exe","PowerRun.exe","Allpatch2.exe"))
    or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
        and ProcessCommandLine has "MpPreference"
        and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("DisableRealtimeMonitoring","EnableControlledFolderAccess Disabled","ExclusionProcess","ExclusionPath"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| where (NewProcessName has_any ("kavrmvr.exe","OpenArk64.exe","PowerRun.exe","Allpatch2.exe"))
    or (NewProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
        and CommandLine has "MpPreference"
        and CommandLine has_any ("DisableRealtimeMonitoring","EnableControlledFolderAccess Disabled","ExclusionProcess","ExclusionPath"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

The Gentlemen Windows Defender disabled via Policy registry keys AIInstallation High
Detects The Gentlemen disabling Defender by writing the policy registry values DisableAntiSpyware / DisableBehaviorMonitoring / DisableOnAccessProtection / DisableScanOnRealtimeEnable = 1 under the Windows Defender policy hive (via .reg import). Distinct registry-telemetry pivot from the PowerShell-based tampering. Rationale: Registry keys and values are taken verbatim from the article's exported .reg block under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows Defender. Value-name + data=1 under the policy hive is high-fidelity tampering. Falcon left empty: these policy keys are not reliably captured by the AsepValueUpdate (autostart) event the FDR exposes. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/the-gentlemen-ransomware-defense-evasion-ttps • https://s2w.inc/en/resource/detail/1053
ATT&CKT1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Group Policy legitimately disabling Defender on hosts managed by a third-party AV (DisableAntiSpyware pushed by GPO)
  • Gold-image build process turning off Defender before installing the enterprise AV
  • Admin troubleshooting an AV conflict by temporarily setting DisableBehaviorMonitoring
  • MDM/SCCM baseline applying a Defender configuration
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("gpscript.exe","svchost.exe","ccmexec.exe","WmiPrvSE.exe")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm whether a sanctioned GPO/MDM pushed the value (InitiatingProcess = svchost/gpscript) versus an interactive process like reg.exe/regedit/cmd.exe run by a user. Check if a different enterprise AV is the intended owner. 2) CONTAIN: Revert the registry values, force a gpupdate, isolate the host if the writer was interactive/non-admin. 3) HUNT: Correlate same-host BYOVD driver loads, Set-MpPreference tampering, and C2 to 81.177.215.15:9443; expect ransomware staging shortly after.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\Policies\Microsoft\Windows Defender"
| where RegistryValueName in~ ("DisableAntiSpyware","DisableBehaviorMonitoring","DisableOnAccessProtection","DisableScanOnRealtimeEnable")
| where RegistryValueData == "1"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Policies\Microsoft\Windows Defender"
| where RegistryValue in~ ("DisableAntiSpyware","DisableBehaviorMonitoring","DisableOnAccessProtection","DisableScanOnRealtimeEnable")
| where RegistryValueData in ("1","0x1","DWORD (0x00000001)")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

The Gentlemen ransomware deployment via deploy_gpo.ps1 / NETLOGON staging AIActions on Objectives High
Detects The Gentlemen's domain-wide lateral movement: execution of the custom deploy_gpo.ps1 GPO-deployment script and staging of the ransomware executable on the NETLOGON share for simultaneous distribution to domain hosts. Rationale: Uses the article's named lateral-movement script deploy_gpo.ps1 and the NETLOGON-share distribution method. The deploy_gpo.ps1 filename is unique to this actor; NETLOGON-staged .exe execution corroborated by SOC Prime and Trend Micro GPO-abuse reporting. Cross-checked against: • https://socprime.com/blog/the-gentlemen-ransomware-detection/ • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/i/unmasking-the-gentlemen-ransomware.html
ATT&CKT1484.001 T1570
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate logon-script .exe staged in NETLOGON (e.g. drive-mapping or inventory tool) executed at user logon
  • AD admin running a sanctioned GPO-deployment PowerShell script with a different name (excluded by deploy_gpo.ps1 specificity)
  • Software-distribution tooling that copies installers into SYSVOL/NETLOGON
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has @"\NETLOGON\" and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("userinit.exe","gpscript.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("logon.exe","mapdrives","inventory"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Open deploy_gpo.ps1 / the NETLOGON-staged binary and hash it against the article's ransomware MD5 list; identify the privileged account and source DC that staged it. 2) CONTAIN: Remove the malicious GPO and the NETLOGON/SYSVOL payload immediately, disable the abused account, and block the ransomware hash org-wide before logon-driven execution spreads. 3) HUNT: Enumerate all hosts that pulled the NETLOGON object, check for PsExec-based execution of the same binary, BYOVD driver loads, and shadow-copy deletion as pre-encryption signals.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "deploy_gpo.ps1"
    or (ProcessCommandLine has @"\NETLOGON\" and ProcessCommandLine has ".exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| where CommandLine has "deploy_gpo.ps1"
    or (CommandLine has "\\NETLOGON\\" and CommandLine has ".exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK

    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

        CommandLine|contains:

    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote

      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high

status: experimental
description: |

    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase

            - 'DownloadString'

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
—
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07

            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'

level: high

Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Critical

Microsoft Removes 119 Edge Extensions That Hid Malware in Images and Fonts

The Hacker News
2026-06-29 11 use cases 6 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Microsoft has shut down a long-running malicious extension operation on the Edge Add-ons store that hid its payloads inside ordinary image and font files, then woke up days after install to steal credentials and run ad fraud. The company calls it&nbsp;StegoAd, a mash-up of steganography and adware, and ties 119 extensions to a single threat actor it says has been active since at least 2021.
